hook.text: The American West is in a megadrought — the driest 22-year period in at least 1,200 years.

buildup.text: Lake Mead, the largest US reservoir, dropped so low that a sunken boat from the 1980s surfaced.

discovery.text: Tree ring data shows the West had megadroughts before — but none worsened by human warming.

twist.text: 42% of the current drought severity is directly attributed to human-caused climate change.

climax.text: States are now fighting over shrinking Colorado River water — the old agreements no longer work.

punchline.text: The river that built the West is running out of promises.

quiz.question: How long has the current American West megadrought lasted?

details.summary: Megadroughts are extreme dry periods lasting decades or longer. The American Southwest is experiencing its worst megadrought in 1,200 years, shrinking reservoirs like Lake Mead and Lake Powell. Climate change is intensifying drought by increasing evaporation and reducing snowpack.
details.whyItMatters: Megadroughts threaten water supply, agriculture, and hydropower for tens of millions of people. They reveal the limits of infrastructure designed for wetter historical conditions.
takeaways: The western US is in its worst megadrought in 1,200 years
Lake Mead has dropped to critically low levels
Warming increases evaporation and reduces snowpack

faq.question: What is the difference between a drought and a megadrought?
faq.answer: A drought typically lasts months to a few years. A megadrought persists for decades, fundamentally altering water availability across an entire region. Tree-ring records show the current western US drought is more severe than anything in over a millennium.

faq.question: What will happen if Lake Mead keeps dropping?
faq.answer: Below critical levels, Hoover Dam can no longer generate hydroelectric power, and water deliveries to Nevada, Arizona, and California face severe cuts. At dead pool the dam cannot release water at all, threatening supply for over 25 million people.
